title: Does Corporate Governance Matter in Competitive Industries?
research_question: Does the strength of corporate governance have differential effects on firm operating performance and managerial behavior depending on the level of product market competition in the firm's industry? Specifically, when external disciplinary pressure on managers is weakened, do firms in non-competitive industries experience greater deterioration in performance and increased managerial slack than firms in competitive industries, and which specific agency problems (e.g., empire building vs. enjoying a 'quiet life') does competition mitigate?
data_description: The primary data source is Standard and Poor's Compustat, covering U.S.-incorporated and U.S.-located firms from 1976 to 1995, yielding 10,960 firms and 81,095 firm-year observations (regulated utilities, SIC 4900-4999, are excluded). Key variables include return on assets (EBITDA/total assets), size, age, leverage, capital expenditures, asset and PPE growth, SG&A, advertising, R&D, costs of goods sold, and wages (labor expenses per employee). Competition is measured primarily by the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index based on 3-digit SIC codes computed from Compustat sales, with robustness checks using 2- and 4-digit HHIs, asset-based HHIs, Census HHI (manufacturing), industry net profit margin (Lerner index), and import penetration. Acquisition data come from SDC (1979 onward), stock returns from CRSP, and earnings management proxies follow Dechow-Sloan-Sweeney and Teoh-Welch-Wong. The unit of observation is the firm-year.
institutional_context: The setting exploits the staggered enactment of 30 state-level business combination (BC) laws passed between 1985 and 1991. These laws impose a three- to five-year moratorium on mergers and asset sales between a large shareholder and the firm once the shareholder's stake crosses a prespecified threshold, thereby blocking corporate raiders from accessing target assets to repay acquisition debt and making hostile takeovers substantially more difficult. Because BC laws apply based on a firm's state of incorporation—often distinct from its state of operations or industry—they create variation in the strength of the external takeover-based disciplining mechanism that is largely orthogonal to local economic conditions and industry shocks. Anecdotal evidence (Romano 1987) indicates these laws were typically passed under pressure from a single firm facing an imminent takeover threat, rather than broad industry coalitions. Newspaper-report dates for 19 of the 30 laws are also used to identify the moment when news about each law first became public.
